evidence.quote: the park’s diverse forested karst landscape, the Green and Nolin rivers

evidence.quote: It is in these underlying massive limestone layers that the human-explorable caves of the region have naturally developed.

evidence.claim: The route begins at Hines’s former home on US 31W.
evidence.quote: Beginning in Bowling Green (Warren County) on US 31W at the former home of Duncan Hines

evidence.claim: His connection with travel began well before the cake mixes: as a salesman for a Chicago printer, he ate his way across the country.
evidence.quote: Hines worked as a traveling salesman for a Chicago printer, and he had eaten many meals on the road across the United States by 1935

evidence.claim: He and his wife Florence compiled restaurant recommendations for friends, then turned the popular list into Adventures in Good Eating in 1935.
evidence.quote: Hines and his wife Florence began assembling a list for friends of several hundred good restaurants around the country. The list became popular and he began selling the paperback book Adventures in Good Eating (1935)

evidence.claim: By 1953, Hines had sold rights to his name and book title to Roy H. Park; Nebraska Consolidated Mills licensed the name and developed the first Duncan Hines cake mixes.
evidence.quote: By 1953, Hines sold the right to use his name and the title of his book to Roy H. Park to form Hines-Park Foods, which licensed the name to a number of food-related businesses. The cake mix license was sold to Nebraska Consolidated Mills in Omaha, Nebraska, which developed and sold the first Duncan Hines cake mixes.

evidence.claim: After his death, a section of US 31W north of Bowling Green was named Duncan Hines Highway.
evidence.quote: a portion of U.S. Route 31W north of the city was named the Duncan Hines Highway after his death.

evidence.quote: Smiths Grove-Hays Road, KY 101, Little Knob Road, Oakland Dixie Highway

evidence.quote: KY 187 to Sunfish , KY 238 to Bee Spring, KY 259 and KY 728 to near Demunbruns Store, KY 1827 and KY 1352 to the Mammoth Cave National Park Boundary, then via Maple Springs Ranger Station Road to the Green River Ferry

evidence.claim: Pig sits at the junction of KY 259 and KY 422 in southern Edmonson County.
evidence.quote: Pig is an unincorporated community in southern Edmonson County

evidence.claim: Pig sits at the junction of KY 259 and KY 422 in southern Edmonson County.
evidence.quote: Pig is located at the intersection of KY 259 and KY 422.

evidence.claim: Its name followed a disagreement over what to call the town: a resident mentioned a small hog he had seen on the road, and Pig was accepted.
evidence.quote: The town was named after disputes over which name to choose. A resident stated he saw a small hog on the road. The name of "Pig" was then accepted.

evidence.claim: Beyond KY 422’s northern end, the road continues as Park Boundary Road, also called Cedar Sink Road, toward KY 70 inside Mammoth Cave National Park.
evidence.quote: Park Boundary Road (also known as Cedar Sink Road) is a continuation of KY 422's roadbed north of that route's northern terminus leading to KY 70 within the nearby Mammoth Cave National Park.

evidence.claim: Green River Ferry began in 1934 and is the last active river ferry in Mammoth Cave National Park.
evidence.quote: The Green River Ferry was first developed in 1934 and is the last remaining active river ferry in the park.

evidence.claim: The Green River runs through the park, receiving the Nolin River just inside its boundary.
evidence.quote: The Green River runs through the park, with a tributary called the Nolin River feeding into the Green just inside the park.

evidence.claim: It carries vehicles, hikers and cyclists, and gives county residents a more direct commute to communities south of the river.
evidence.quote: It provides shuttle service for vehicles, hikers and bikers from one side of the river to the other. It is also a link for community residents within the county to have an easier commute to local communities on the south side of the river.

evidence.claim: Beside the crossing, the parking area connects with the one-mile Accessible Echo River Spring loop through the forest.
evidence.quote: The Green River Ferry parking area also offers access to the Accessible Echo River Spring hiking trail, a one-mile wheelchair accessible loop path through the forest.

evidence.claim: Benches and viewpoints stand along the trail, while a kayak and canoe launch lies just upstream of the ferry.
evidence.quote: There are picnic tables at the trailhead and benches and viewpoints along the trail.

evidence.claim: Benches and viewpoints stand along the trail, while a kayak and canoe launch lies just upstream of the ferry.
evidence.quote: A kayak and canoe launch is located adjacent to the parking area near the Green River just upstream from the ferry crossing.

evidence.claim: Kyrock shipped road paving by river.
evidence.quote: the company mined, processed, and shipped hundreds of tons of rock asphalt by means of steamboat transportation on both the Nolin and Green Rivers. This was done to eventually pave roadways

evidence.claim: The name Kyrock came from the company’s own name, Kentucky Rock Asphalt Company.
evidence.quote: the Kentucky Rock Asphalt Company, which the town's name, Kyrock, is derived from.

evidence.claim: In the 1920s, the Kentucky Rock Asphalt Company mined and processed rock asphalt here, then sent hundreds of tons away by steamboat on the Nolin and Green rivers.
evidence.quote: During the Kentucky Rock and Asphalt Company's heyday in the 1920s as Edmonson County's largest local business, the company mined, processed, and shipped hundreds of tons of rock asphalt by means of steamboat transportation on both the Nolin and Green Rivers.

evidence.claim: The company built a town with schools, a church and a commissary.
evidence.quote: the company also constructed an elementary and high school building, a Methodist church, two hotels, a commissary

evidence.claim: Competition from cheaper petroleum-based asphalt and higher shipping costs helped end the operation in 1957.
evidence.quote: Higher costs to pave with asphalt resulted in the end of the company with the advent of petroleum-based asphalt, which was a lower-cost method of paving. As a result of stiffened competition with other asphalt companies and higher shipping costs, Kentucky Rock Asphalt Company was shut down in 1957.

evidence.claim: The original water tower and a concrete footbridge foundation over Pigeon Creek remain from the town.
evidence.quote: Aside from the original water tower, the only remnants of the town in the present day is a concrete foundation for a swinging footbridge over Pigeon Creek.
